paragraphs.text: Lesson 17. A mysterious movie. Listen to Paula and Jack discuss the movie they just saw and
answer the comprehension questions based on their conversation.
That movie was weird, don't you think?
What do you mean? I thought it was terrific. It's not often you see a movie with such a great
twist at the end.
That's what makes it so creepy. I was positive the man in the black suit was the killer, but
it turned out to be the high school history teacher Mrs. Kepler.
I was really thrown for a loop. Mrs. Kepler seems so sweet there was nothing sinister about
her whatsoever, but she was killing off the faculty one by one.
You know, on the way out of the theatre I overheard someone saying the movie was based
on a true story.
No way. If there was a killing spree like that we would have heard about it. I mean come
on. She killed 16 people? That kind of thing would have been all over the news.
I didn't say the case was recent. The person was saying it all went down in a small European
town in 1974. The writer dug up the story when he visited Europe. He just changed a few
details to make the movie more dramatic.
Ugh. I'll never look at the history teacher the same way again.
The real mystery was her motive. The movie left us hanging on that part. Now I'm going to
look up the case. What was Mrs. Kepler's background? What drove her to kill so many people?
Maybe there was no reason. Could be she was just an evil person masquerading as a kind motherly
teacher. I don't understand why you're intrigued by these cases.
But aren't you curious?
Paula when Mrs. Kepler confessed it made my blood turn cold. I really pegged her as a harmless
old lady who wouldn't hurt a fly. I was fooled and that scares me. I would have trusted Mrs.
Kepler just like those people in the movie did. And I would have ended up six feet under two.
And that's what makes me shudder.
We also got to find out who the man in black was. The movie never revealed his identity.
Uh oh. I can see by that look on your face you're not going to leave me alone unless
I help you research this movie.
There's still so many loose ends in the story. Mrs. Kepler was pretty old and frail. How did
she manage to hide the bodies? Hey, the man in black might have been Mrs. Kepler's accomplice.
He could still be prowling the streets, just lurking in the dark until he finds his next
victim.
Don't say that. Now I'm going to have nightmares for sure.
Let's learn the vocabulary from this conversation about a movie. Jack says the movie was weird.
The word weird means strange or unusual. But Paula enjoyed it. She says it's not often you
see a movie with such a great twist at the end. In this context, a twist is an unexpected
change of events, for example, in the story of a movie or book.
But Jack says that's what makes it so creepy. The word creepy means it produces a sensation
of uneasiness or fear. It's disturbing. It makes you uncomfortable.
When the identity of the killer was revealed in the movie, Paula was really thrown for a
loop. This expression, I was thrown for a loop, means I was completely surprised, confused,
and maybe even a little bit upset. Mrs. Kepler seemed so sweet, there was nothing sinister
about her whatsoever. The word sinister means threatening or suggesting evil. But she was
killing off the faculty one by one. The word faculty refers to the group of teachers at
a school or college. Paula then adds that she overheard a conversation on the way out of
the theater. The word overheard means she heard part of someone else's conversation. The
two people were not talking to her, but she heard or listened to them talking to each other.
Jack doubts that the movie was based on a true story because, he says, if there was a killing
spree like that, we would have heard about it. A killing spree means a lot of people killed
in a short amount of time. And Paula replies that these events all went down in a small
European town in 1974. This phrase, it all went down, is a slang way to say it all happened.
According to Paula, the writer dug up the story when he visited Europe.
Dugg up the story means he discovered some hidden or little known information.
One thing the movie didn't explain was Mrs. Kepler's motive. Paula says, the movie left
us hanging on that part. Left us hanging means it didn't fully explain it. It left us in suspense,
wondering about or curious about the answer. Paula wants to find out about Mrs. Kepler's
background and discover what drove her to kill so many people. Drove her means motivated her.
Jack suggests that there was no reason. Perhaps she was just an evil person masquerading as a kind
means pretending to be. Jack doesn't understand why Paula is so intrigued by these cases.
The word intrigued means extremely interested. Jack says that when Mrs. Kepler confessed,
it made his blood turn cold. This is an idiom that means it caused an intense sensation of fear.
Jack really pegged Mrs. Kepler as a harmless old lady. Pagged her is an informal way to say
classified her. He formed an opinion about her as a particular type of person.
A harmless old lady who wouldn't hurt a fly. This expression wouldn't hurt a fly describes a
person who would not hurt anybody. However, Jack was fooled. Fold means deceived or tricked.
He says, I would have trusted Mrs. Kepler and I would have ended up six feet under two.
Six feet under is a slang way to say dead. An expression like this is typically only used
when talking about death in a casual or joking way. Don't use it when somebody's loved one has died.
Jack says, that's what makes me shudder. The word shudder means shake with fear.
Paula wants to find out more because she says there are still so many loose ends in the story.
Loose ends means unresolved issues. For example, Mrs. Kepler was pretty old and frail,
so how did she manage to hide the bodies? The word frail means weak. We usually use frail
when a person's body is weakened by old age or disease. Paula suggests that the man in black
could have been Mrs. Kepler's accomplice. The word accomplice means a person who is a partner or
helper in a crime. Paula then says he could still be prowling the streets.
Prowling means going around looking for a victim for somebody to attack.
This man might be lurking in the dark until he finds his next victim.
Lurking means existing unobserved, often in a threatening way. Jack exclaims,
don't say that. Now I'm going to have nightmares for sure.
Nightmares are scary dreams. That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
